The authors deleted an extremely large stretch of titin that is believed to be responsible for passive elasticity, and mice with that deletion indeed turn out to have a reduction in passive stiffness. The mice themselves are surprisingly normal, likely due to compensating changes in the muscle. The study is very relevant and experiments are expertly performed.

The manuscript can benefit from a revised discussion ion how the data helps us understand the role of titin in active contraction. For example, Reviewer 3 suggests, based on prior literature, the compensatory changes occur to main the relevant mechanical tension across titin.

Separate reviews (please respond to each point):

Reviewer #1:

In the study by Brynnel and collaborators, the authors generate and characterize very thoroughly a mouse model (Delta112-158) in which the PEVK region of titin is genetically shortened to assess the role of the protein in skeletal muscle passive stiffness. The topic is highly relevant since titin is a main player in the mechanical performance of striated muscle, and because different diseases originate from mutations in the titin gene. Hence, there is a pressing need in the field to understand how the mechanical properties of titin molecules influence the performance of striated muscle. The group has produced before several mouse models in which different segments of titin have been altered. The novelty of the Delta112-158 model comes from the fact that it involves a massive deletion (46 exons) in the PEVK region of the protein, which is believed to be one of the major contributors to the passive mechanical properties of titin. It is very interesting to examine how mice adapt to such a massive deletion in titin, which the authors do in their manuscript combining several top-notch physiology and molecular biology techniques.

The authors provide data supporting the expression of shortened titin in the homozygous Delta112-158 mice, both at the RNA and protein levels. Using super-resolution microscopy on muscle preparations and modelling, the authors confirm that Delta112-158 titin is stiffer than wild-type, as expected. Interestingly, even though higher muscle stiffness is found in Delta112-158 mice, the authors find that mice do well in general terms (including exercise tests). This increased stiffness is found at the level of intact, skinned and KCl/KI-extracted muscle. Indeed, results are in agreement with a prominent role of titin in setting the passive stiffness of skeletal muscle, since the stiffness of Delta112-158 muscles correlates very well with the increase in titin-based stiffness. Titin-based stiffness is deduced from data obtained after KCl/KI extraction, a method that can potentially affect other muscle components. However, they provide nice supporting data obtained with single fibers, which are naturally devoid of extracellular matrix (Figure 5C). The authors also measured active contraction, and found that Delta112-158 mice develop force faster than wild-type mice, with no difference in the maximal force developed.

In our opinion the most striking observation is that there are compensatory changes that enable myocytes to adjust to the shortened titin, e.g. reduced sarcomere length working range and shortened thin filaments, which are accompanied by longitudinal hypertrophy at the muscle level. These adaptations probably lead to normal viability and development of Delta112-158 mice.

Although the characterization of the new model is very thorough already, we believe that there are highly interesting questions to address in the future, such as how is the new sarcomere length working rate set?, how early in development these adjustments occur?, are these adjustments already completed at the embryo stage? It may be interesting also to analyze heterozygous mice to check how myocytes adapt to a titin stiffness imbalance.

We have some concerns regarding the current version of the manuscript:

1) It seems that adaptation in sarcomere length working range can lead to equal working stiffness of titin (and muscle) in wild-type and Delta112-158 mice, which would be a very interesting observation. Can the authors compare stiffness at the sarcomere length working range for both wild-type and Delta112-158 mice? The insets in Figures 3C, 4, and 5 are calculated at the same sarcomere lengths, which can be misleading since sarcomere length working ranges are different for both mice.

2) It is argued in subsection “Active tension” that results with Delta112-158 mice provide evidence against the recently proposed mechanisms of titin folding contributing to active contraction. In our opinion, the arguments raised by the authors do not support this view because they don't take into account the different sarcomere length working ranges (see above). Results in Figure 3C suggest that at the different sarcomere length working ranges (as measured in Figure 7D), both WT and Delta112-158 titin experience very similar forces and hence the expected rate of folding/unfolding in both cases should be very similar.

Minor Comments:

3) The facts that Delta112-158 mice weigh less than wild-type, but have heavier muscles are somehow contradictory. Can the authors provide an explanation? Do Delta112-158 mice have less adipose tissue, less water content, etc? This should be at least discussed and more data provided if already available.

4) It would be nice to describe in the Materials and methods section how the force-sarcomere length relations were calculated (Figure 10B).

5) Some techniques employed by the authors are very specialized. Although the Materials and method section is in general very detailed, it may help to show some illustrative raw data in some cases, for instance the kind of images used to calculate CSA.

6) Subsection “Force-sarcomere length relation”: A-band length instead of width

7) Subsection “Sarcomeres in series and longitudinal hypertrophy”: what does "interaction between genotype and age" refer to? Consider rephrasing.

Reviewer #2:

This is an excellent and comprehensive evaluation of the changes in muscle structure and function in a genetic model, Ttn112-158, of 46 exons deletions in titin's spring region. By shortening titin's spring region, titin became significantly stiffer, and affected passive force (interestingly not active force) in fibers and muscles, and was associated with structural changes (other than just the changes to titin) most remarkably, a shortening of the actin filaments by about 63nm, an increase in fiber lengths, and a vast increase (30%) in serial sarcomeres.

Some small limitations of the study include that:

i) titin stiffness was never measured directly, but was obtained indirectly. Titin stiffness or passive force contribution as a function of sarcomere length can be directly obtained in single myofibrils, thus eliminating any concerns of indirect measurements where titin is deleted from muscles/fibers, and skinning may affect (although apparently not in this preparation), the passive forces.

ii) it has been argued by that titin's stiffness changes/increases upon activation and actin-myosin-based force production. The idea that titin might play a different role in activated muscle compared to passive muscle was not discussed, and with some of the authors having published evidence of a change in titin stiffness with activation/force production/muscle stretch, this might have added to a more complete discussion.

iii) ranges of sarcomere excursions in muscles were derived from fixed (passive) specimens. It is accepted that depending on the muscle and the length of the muscle, fibers and average sarcomere lengths decrease between 5-30% in active compared to passive muscles. If we assume that the Ttn112-158 muscles have greater passive stiffness, then shortening of sarcomeres in these muscles upon activation might be less than for the wild-type muscles. Therefore, the sarcomere excursions between the Ttn112-158 and WT muscles might be closer during active force production than the passive results suggest.

Minor Comments:

The only minor comment I have is regarding a statement in the Introduction section. Here it is said that: "…. and in cerebral palsy patients, titin-based passive stiffness is increased several fold [22, 23]". Reference 22 is not dealing with cerebral palsy, and reference 23 has just one reference to cerebral palsy (Friden and Lieber, 2003). Measurements in that study were performed in single fibers of patients with cerebral palsy, and they found that the elastic modulus of the passive fibers was doubled compared to control. However, fibers do not only give titin stiffness and passive force contributions but an unknown amount of passive force can also come from other sources, which is hard to control and estimate in single fibers.

We just performed a study on single myofibrils from spastic muscles of patients with cerebral palsy and found that single myofibril passive forces (at given sarcomere lengths) and stiffness (at given sarcomere lengths) were about 50% smaller than those of corresponding myofibrils from control subjects. These passive forces are exclusively due to titin in myofibrils. Measuring titin molecular mass, we did not find a difference between the control and cerebral palsy samples. However, when quantifying the amount of titin, we found that the amount of titin was reduced by about 50% in the samples from the cerebral palsy patients compared to control. Unfortunately, our study is still in the review process, and thus does not need to be considered here. But likely, titin-based stiffness, as directly assessed by us, rather than the indirect methods used by Friden and Lieber, 2003, seems much less in patients with cerebral palsy than controls because of a reduction in the amount of titin.

Additional data files and statistical comments:

There is no need (from my point of view) to add additional files and/or to change any of the statistical approaches. They seem perfectly appropriate.

Reviewer #3:

Granzier and colleagues have a long history of designing and characterizing mouse models in which the titin gene has been altered. The phenomenology that emerges from their work is useful in our budding attempts to understand how titin is integrated into the structure of muscle. Their previous models have included deletion of the elastic N2B segment from myofibrils, M-line domains, splicing factors responsible for regulating titin length, and a piece of the PEVK segment. This last paper ("Truncation of titin's elastic PEVK region leads to cardiomyopathy with diastolic dysfunction", Circulation Research, 2009) identified a marked cardiac phenotype and also established that titin was the principal source of muscle elasticity and not its collagen sheath. In the current work, by removing more exons to truncate the PEVK segment by 1180 amino acids, they get new phenotypes, this time in skeletal muscles. While deletion of the C-terminal exons of the PEVK segment (exons 219-225) resulted in a diastolic dysfunction phenotype with increased titin based passive tension (Circ Res, 2009), deletion of the N-terminal PEVK segment here (exons 112-158) caused a very different phenotype where they now observe a shift in several different muscle types, to shorter sarcomere length, shorter thin filaments, and longitudinal hypertrophy where an increased number of sarcomeres spans the same muscle length. It is likely that these adaptations result from a homeostatic change aimed at keeping the mean force per titin at a constant working value. This can be easily pictured by drawing a horizontal line, say at 5 pN, in both panels of Figure 3C and finding the intercepts with the WT and TtnD122-158 mice. It is clear then that to keep the titin working force at the same set-point, the mutant mouse has to work at sarcomere lengths that are shorter by about 0.5 micrometers which is exactly what the authors observe in vivo.

Why is it that the organism places such a premium on keeping the force per titin at a constant value? A likely explanation can be found in Rivas-Pardo et al., 2016 and Eckels et al., 2018 who proposed that titin folding plays a role both in muscle elasticity and contraction. This theory demands that titin operates precisely over a range of forces that straddles the folding probability of the titin Ig domains (~4-8 pN): If the force is too high (>12 pN), folding never occurs, and if it is too low titin is always folded (< 3 pN). In either case, titin folding would not play a role. By contrast, if titin operates in vivo at forces that are on average in the middle of the Ig domain folding probability curve, say ~5-6 pN, then muscle tissue can take advantage of the storage and release of elastic energy that takes place with Ig domain folding. If this were true, muscle physiology would place a high premium on getting titin to operate over a tight range of forces. Indeed, Rivas-Pardo et al., predicted that the optimal sarcomere length in vivo would closely track this fundamental requirement adjusting widely amongst different muscle types, tracking their alternatively spliced differences in stiffness (Figures 5C and 5D in Rivas Pardo et al., 2016).

Unwittingly, the current work by Granzier and colleagues lends strong support to this hypothesis. How the titin operating force is transduced into such large scale adaptations is a work in progress. However, we do know that titin has a force sensor at its C-terminus end (Mayans Nature 1998, Lange Science 2005) and that undergoes force-induced structural changes to activate downstream pathways of gene expression, presumably as a feedback mechanism to control the operating force range. Thus, a coherent view emerges, where a high premium is placed by the organism on exactly controlling the operating force of titin molecules; this has the signature of protein folding under force.

More excitingly, the current work offers an approach for a definitive test of this theory. If all the Ig domains of the proximal I band region were replaced by PEVK segments -while maintaining the same molecular weight-, then titin would be converted into a mostly passive entropic spring. The kinase control would adjust the sarcomere length to restore the correct operating force in all muscles, and the sarcomere would become longer to achieve the correct resting tension per titin, however, there would be no Ig domain folding/unfolding reactions. If under these conditions the peak contractile force remains unchanged, then the mechanical power developed by Ig domain folding plays no role in muscle contraction. However, If Ig domain folding is crucial for muscle contraction, then obviously the peak force would be greatly diminished by the removal of the Ig domains and the experiments would validate the hypothesis. As they stand, the current experiments do not answer this question. Given that the authors have removed only the elastomeric PEVK segment but left the Ig domains intact, the Ig folding mechanisms remains a viable theory.

claims.claim: The adaptation in the physiological sarcomere length range of TtnΔ112-158 mice is remarkably effective at normalizing passive stiffness.
claims.source: That this shift is functionally important can be evaluated by plotting the average passive stiffness of titin in the physiological sarcomere length range. This reveals an identical passive stiffness in the two genotypes (see Figure 12). Thus, the adaptation in the physiological sarcomere length range of the TtnΔ112-158 mice is remarkably effective at normalizing passive stiffness.
claims.evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the analysis shown in Figure 12.

claims.claim: The TtnΔ112-158 mice are likely to have a lower body fat content based on increased muscle weights combined with reduced body weight and normal body size.
claims.source: The increased muscles weights, combined with the reduced body weight and normal body size (revealed by the normal tibia lengths, discussed above), suggests that the TtnΔ112-158 mice are likely to have a lower body fat content.
claims.evidence: The manuscript suggests this based on the combination of measurements.

claims.claim: At the macroscopic scale of a whole muscle contracting at L0, the titin unfolding/refolding mechanism is unlikely to significantly add to the level of tetanic tension.
claims.source: It is possible that the refolding mechanism is not active because passive forces at L0 are too low, in both genotypes. Perhaps, at longer lengths sufficient levels of unfolding might take place, due to the higher passive tensions, and the mechanism is operational. Presently we conclude that at the macroscopic scale of a whole muscle contracting at L0, the titin unfolding/refolding mechanism is unlikely to significantly add to the level of tetanic tension.
claims.evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the active tension measurements.

claims.claim: The more rapid force development in TtnΔ112-158 muscle is speculated to be due to the higher passive tension increasing the thick filament ON state, which accelerates force generation when a muscle is stimulated.
claims.source: Because no fiber type switch was found in TtnΔ112-158 muscles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) it is unlikely that this increased speed of force development is due to the expression of faster fiber types. Instead, we speculate that this more rapid force development is due to the higher passive tension in TtnΔ112-158 muscle that increases the thick filament ON state and that this accelerates force generation when a muscle is stimulated.
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates this mechanism based on the data.

claims.claim: In TtnΔ112-158 mice, the nebulin-free distal segment of the thin filament is speculated to be reduced in length in response to the shift in the sarcomere length working range.
claims.source: Considering that the thin filament contains a distal nebulin-free segment (Littlefield and Fowler, 2008), we speculate that in TtnΔ112-158 mice this nebulin-free distal segment is reduced in length, in response to the shift in the sarcomere length working range.
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates this mechanism based on the thin filament length data and citation (Littlefield and Fowler, 2008).

claims.claim: Normalizing function through the addition of approximately 30% sarcomeres is energetically costly, as suggested by the reduced weight of TtnΔ112-158 mice.
claims.source: Normalizing function through the addition of ~30% sarcomeres is energetically costly, as suggested by the reduced weight of the TtnΔ112-158 mice (Figure 1D), and ultimately might be detrimental.
claims.evidence: The manuscript suggests this based on the body weight data.

claims.claim: The TtnΔ112-158 model provides a unique opportunity to test the effects of altered titin-based tension on active muscle function.
claims.source: The TtnΔ112-158 model also provides a unique opportunity to test the effects of altered titin-based tension on active muscle function.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this opportunity.

claims.claim: Titin might store elastic energy by unfolding Ig domains in passive muscle and generate forces through their refolding during contraction that add to active force.
claims.source: For example, titin might store elastic energy by unfolding Ig domains in passive muscle. Through their refolding during contraction, titin might generate forces that add to the active force (Eckels et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a proposed mechanism (Eckels et al., 2018).

claims.claim: An alternative mechanism consists of titin-based effects on thick filament structure that contribute to activating the thick filament.
claims.source: An alternative mechanism consists of titin-based effects on thick filament structure that contribute to activating the thick filament (Piazzesi et al., 2018; Fusi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites proposed mechanisms (Piazzesi et al., 2018; Fusi et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Within the physiological length range of skeletal muscle, titin's contribution to whole muscle stiffness is dominant, analogous to cardiac muscle.
claims.source: Within the physiological length range of skeletal muscle, however, titin's contribution to whole muscle stiffness is dominant. This is analogous to cardiac muscle where titin also dominates within the physiological sarcomere length (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The manuscript concludes this and draws an analogy to cardiac muscle with citations (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).

claims.claim: An advantage of titin dominating passive stiffness is that this allows for rapid regulation through intracellular signaling mechanisms that post-translationally modify titin's molecular spring region.
claims.source: An advantage of titin dominating passive stiffness is that this allows for rapid regulation through intracellular signaling mechanisms that post-translationally modify titin's molecular spring region (Hidalgo and Granzier, 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this advantage with citation support (Hidalgo and Granzier, 2013).

claims.claim: At sarcomere lengths at or beyond the physiological range limit, the ECM stiffness greatly increases and functions as a brake on the movement range of muscle.
claims.source: This does not mean that the ECM is unimportant for longitudinal stiffness. At sarcomere lengths at or beyond the physiological range limit, the ECM stiffness greatly increases and functions as a brake on the movement range of muscle.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the role of ECM at extreme lengths.

claims.claim: The targeting strategy used homologous recombination to replace exons 112–158 (chr2:76,839,202–76,867,333).
claims.source: The targeting strategy used homologous recombination to replace exons 112–158 (chr2:76,839,202–76,867,333) with the exon numbers from orthologous human titin exons.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the targeting strategy with genomic coordinates.

claims.claim: The TtnΔ112-158 deletion corresponds to a deletion of 47 PEVK exons, encoding 1586 amino acids or 181.7 kDa.
claims.source: The TtnΔ112-158 deletion corresponds to a deletion of 47 PEVK exons, encoding 1586 amino acids or 181.7 kDa.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides specific details about the deletion size.

claims.claim: The passive stiffness of titin and ECM were both significantly increased in TtnΔ112-158 EDL muscle, but the titin stiffness far exceeded the ECM stiffness, approximately 5-fold in WT and approximately 10-fold in TtnΔ112-158 muscle.
claims.source: The stiffness of titin and ECM were both significantly increased in TtnΔ112-158 EDL muscle but the titin stiffness far exceeded the ECM stiffness, ~5-fold in WT and ~10-fold in TtnΔ112-158 muscle (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with specific fold-changes and figure reference.

claims.claim: The WT mice operate on the descending limb and part of the plateau of the force-sarcomere length relation, while TtnΔ112-158 muscle starts out on the plateau and shortens on the ascending limb.
claims.source: The WT mice operate on the descending limb and part of the plateau, but in contrast, the TtnΔ112-158 muscle starts out on the plateau and shortens on the ascending limb.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the different operating ranges on the force-SL curve.

claims.claim: The physiological sarcomere length range of the diaphragm was 2.85 μm to 2.22 μm in WT mice but only 2.37 μm to 1.88 μm in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
claims.source: Results reveal that the TtnΔ112-158 mice had a significantly reduced sarcomere length both during expiration and inspiration (Figure 8B); the physiological sarcomere length range of the diaphragm was 2.85 μm to 2.22 μm in WT mice but only 2.37 μm to 1.88 μm in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides specific sarcomere length ranges.

claims.claim: Two-way ANOVA reveals a significantly increased number of sarcomeres in single fibers in all studied muscle types in TtnΔ112-158 mice, with an average increase of 34%.
claims.source: This revealed a significant and large increase (~30%) in the number of sarcomeres in all examined TtnΔ112-158 muscles (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this with statistical analysis; Figure 9 shows average increase of 34%.

claims.source: A two-way ANOVA analysis with age and genotype as factors revealed that in most muscle types, both genotype and age had a significant effect on muscle weight but with no significant interaction between genotype and age.

claims.source: This indicates that age similarly affected muscle weights of WT and TtnΔ112-158 mice.

claims.source: Clearly, future work is needed to elucidate the mechanisms that underlie the serial addition of sarcomeres. This work should focus on changes that occur at an early age when the longitudinal growth that increases the number of series sarcomeres is not yet complete.

The mechano-signaling mechanism identified recently that involves an increased strain on titin's molecular spring as well as the upregulation of titin-binding proteins (van der Pijl et al., 2018) is a good candidate.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes this as a candidate mechanism with citation (van der Pijl et al., 2018).

claims.source: We speculate that the underlying signaling mechanisms that cause longitudinal hypertrophy are only transiently active and that these mechanisms are 'dialed down' when the increase in the number of sarcomeres in series has been accomplished (and titin's strain has been normalized).

results.result: A viable TtnΔ112-158 mouse model was successfully created by deleting 47 PEVK exons (exons 112-158) from titin's I-band region, resulting in a skeletal-muscle-specific effect. Homozygous mice followed Mendelian genetics, survived without obvious phenotype for up to 1 year, and had normal skeleton size.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21, C76-C77 collectively demonstrate successful creation of the mouse model with appropriate characterization. The deletion is well-documented (genomic coordinates, protein size), viability is confirmed (Mendelian ratios, survival), and skeletal-muscle specificity is established through exon expression patterns in cardiac tissue. The data in Figures 1A-D provide strong supporting evidence.

results.result: TtnΔ112-158 mice had normal body weight at 60 days but developed significant weight reduction with age, while maintaining normal skeleton size as indicated by identical tibia lengths compared to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by two-way ANOVA showing significant genotype effect on body weight across ages (Figure 1D) and no difference in tibia length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The statistical analysis is appropriate and the measurements are straightforward.

results.result: Protein analysis confirmed that T1 titin has higher gel mobility in TtnΔ112-158 mice while T2 mobility is unchanged, and total titin expression levels remain normal across all muscle types studied.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by gel electrophoresis data (Figure 1E) and quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The higher T1 mobility is consistent with the expected 181 kDa deletion, and unchanged T2 mobility is explained by T2 lacking the targeted PEVK segment. Expression analysis shows no compensatory changes.

results.result: RNA sequencing confirmed absence of PEVK exons 112-158 in TtnΔ112-158 transcripts across all three muscle types, with minimal compensatory splicing changes except for consistent upregulation of Z-disk exons 12-13 and PEVK exon 159. The PEVK segment was reduced from ~1600 to ~420 residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are well-supported by comprehensive RNAseq data (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1). PSI analysis quantitatively demonstrates the deletion and minimal off-target effects. The calculated PEVK residue numbers are based on appropriate methodology. The similarity across muscle types is notable and well-documented.

results.result: Super-resolution microscopy measurements showed reduced PEVK segment extension in TtnΔ112-158 mice, and wormlike chain modeling predicted greatly increased titin-based stiffness compared to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by SR-SIM measurements (Figure 3A-B) and biophysical modeling (Figure 3C). The methodology is appropriate, using antibodies flanking the PEVK segment. The WLC modeling uses established parameters and the prediction logically follows from the shortened PEVK segment. However, this is a prediction requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Passive tension measurements in intact diaphragm, EDL, and soleus muscles showed much steeper increases with sarcomere length in TtnΔ112-158 mice, with passive stiffness increased approximately 5-10 fold in the physiological sarcomere length range (2.45-2.75 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are strongly supported by direct mechanical measurements on intact muscles (Figure 4). The methodology is sound, with appropriate sarcomere length determination and stiffness calculation. The several-fold increase is consistent across all three muscle types studied, providing robust evidence.

results.result: Skinning had minimal effect on passive tension, and KCl/KI extraction experiments demonstrated that titin-based tension dominates over ECM-based tension in both WT and TtnΔ112-158 muscles within the physiological sarcomere length range. Titin stiffness was increased ~5-fold in TtnΔ112-158 while ECM stiffness increased but remained much lower.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42, C78 are supported by systematic extraction experiments (Figure 5). The validation using single fibers (which lack ECM) to confirm that KCl/KI extraction specifically removes titin-based tension is a critical control. The quantitative comparison shows titin stiffness exceeds ECM stiffness ~5-10 fold, directly addressing a major controversy in the field.

results.result: Maximal active tension was unaffected by genotype in all muscle types studied, but the time to half-maximal tension was significantly reduced in all TtnΔ112-158 muscle types. This occurred without changes in myosin isoform composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by force-frequency measurements (Figure 6) and myosin isoform analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The lack of effect on maximal tension is important for ruling out certain proposed mechanisms. The faster force development without fiber type changes suggests a titin-mediated mechanism, though the exact mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: Exercise performance was not impaired in TtnΔ112-158 mice, with no differences in voluntary free-wheel running speed/distance or maximal treadmill performance including VO2 consumption.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by comprehensive exercise testing (Figure 7). The lack of functional impairment despite dramatically increased passive stiffness is surprising and suggests successful adaptation. However, the manuscript notes these are female mice, and sex-specific effects should be considered.

results.result: TtnΔ112-158 mice showed a shifted physiological sarcomere length working range to shorter lengths in diaphragm (2.85-2.22 μm in WT vs 2.37-1.88 μm in TtnΔ112-158) and peripheral muscles, while maintaining normal diaphragm strain amplitude during respiration.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52, C80 are supported by perfusion-fixation studies combined with ultrasound imaging (Figure 8). The methodology is rigorous, fixing muscles in known physiological states. The shift to shorter sarcomere lengths is consistent across multiple muscle types and represents a major adaptive response.

results.result: Single fiber measurements revealed significantly increased fiber lengths (13.5%) and a large increase (~30-34%) in the number of sarcomeres in series in all examined TtnΔ112-158 muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54, C81 are supported by direct measurements on dissected fibers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 9). The methodology is appropriate, using laser diffraction for sarcomere length and calculating sarcomere number from fiber length. The ~30% increase is substantial and consistent across muscle types, providing the mechanism for the shifted sarcomere length range.

results.result: Most TtnΔ112-158 muscle types showed significantly increased muscle weight relative to WT controls across multiple ages, without increased cross-sectional area, indicating longitudinal muscle growth. Two-way ANOVA showed both genotype and age effects on muscle weight with no significant interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C57-C58, C82-C83 are supported by systematic muscle weight measurements (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 1) and cross-sectional area analysis (Figure 10D). The statistical analysis is appropriate. The lack of genotype-age interaction suggests the hypertrophy occurs early and is maintained. The inference that increased weight is due to longitudinal growth is logical given the lack of CSA increase.

results.result: Thin filament length was significantly reduced from 1165 nm to 1102 nm in TtnΔ112-158 diaphragm. Force-sarcomere length modeling showed that WT mice operate on the descending limb while TtnΔ112-158 mice operate on the plateau and ascending limb, with average forces within working ranges of 91% (WT) and 96% (TtnΔ112-158) of maximum.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61, C79 are supported by SR-SIM measurements of thin filament length (Figure 11A) and theoretical force-SL modeling (Figure 11B). The thin filament shortening is a novel finding that compensates for the shifted sarcomere length range. The modeling is based on established principles and measured parameters. However, the force-SL predictions are theoretical and would benefit from direct experimental validation.

results.result: The upregulation of Z-disk exons 12 and 13 is proposed to be triggered by increased titin-based tension to mechanically strengthen the Z-disk region when titin stiffness is high.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is a mechanistic proposal based on the observation of Z-disk exon upregulation and the absence of fiber type switching (C46). While the reasoning is logical, this is explicitly stated as a proposal/speculation without direct experimental validation of the mechanism. The claim requires functional studies to test whether these exons actually strengthen the Z-disk under high tension.

results.result: The adaptation in physiological sarcomere length range is remarkably effective at normalizing passive stiffness, with identical passive stiffness in the two genotypes when measured within their respective physiological ranges.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by analysis shown in Figure 12, which demonstrates that despite dramatically different stiffness at identical sarcomere lengths, the operating stiffness within physiological ranges is normalized. This is a key finding showing the functional importance of the sarcomere number adaptation.

results.result: TtnΔ112-158 mice are likely to have lower body fat content based on increased muscle weights combined with reduced body weight and normal body size.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is an inference based on the combination of reduced body weight (C23), increased muscle weight (C55), and normal skeleton size (C24). While the logic is reasonable, this is explicitly stated as a suggestion without direct measurement of body composition. Body fat measurement would be needed to confirm this inference.

results.result: At the macroscopic scale of whole muscle contracting at L0, the titin unfolding/refolding mechanism is unlikely to significantly add to tetanic tension, despite this being a proposed mechanism in the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C66 and C71 are supported by the lack of increased active tension in TtnΔ112-158 muscles despite higher passive tension at L0 (Figure 6B). The manuscript appropriately tests a hypothesis from the literature (C71, citing Eckels et al., 2018) and provides evidence against its significance at the whole muscle level. However, the authors note the mechanism might operate at longer lengths.

results.result: The more rapid force development in TtnΔ112-158 muscle is speculated to result from higher passive tension increasing the thick filament ON state, which accelerates force generation upon stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C72 represent speculation about mechanism based on the observed faster force development (C45) and literature on thick filament regulation (C72, citing Piazzesi et al., 2018; Fusi et al., 2016). While the hypothesis is reasonable and consistent with the data, it is explicitly stated as speculation without direct experimental validation of thick filament state or structure.

results.result: The nebulin-free distal segment of the thin filament is speculated to be reduced in length in TtnΔ112-158 mice in response to the shifted sarcomere length working range.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is speculation about the mechanism of thin filament shortening. While the thin filament shortening is well-documented (C59), and nebulin expression is unchanged (Figure 11—figure supplement 1), the specific mechanism involving the nebulin-free segment is proposed without direct experimental evidence. This would require detailed structural analysis of the thin filament pointed end.

results.result: The extensive adaptations required to normalize passive stiffness through serial sarcomere addition indicate that increased passive stiffness is functionally detrimental and must be avoided, though this adaptation is energetically costly as suggested by reduced body weight.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C84 represent interpretations of the extensive adaptations observed (sarcomere addition, thin filament shortening, Z-disk strengthening). The conclusion that increased stiffness is detrimental is logical given the magnitude of compensatory responses. The energetic cost inference is supported by reduced body weight (C23) despite increased muscle mass (C55), though direct metabolic measurements would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Within the physiological sarcomere length range, titin dominates whole muscle passive stiffness analogous to cardiac muscle, allowing rapid regulation through post-translational modifications. ECM functions as a brake at extreme sarcomere lengths beyond the physiological range.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 represent major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. C73 is directly supported by the extraction experiments (C38-C42). C74 is a logical inference about regulatory advantages with appropriate citation. C75 is supported by the observation that ECM stiffness increases at longer lengths (Figure 5D). These conclusions appropriately integrate the findings with broader muscle physiology.

results.result: Future work should focus on early developmental changes to elucidate mechanisms of serial sarcomere addition, with mechano-signaling involving titin strain and titin-binding proteins as a candidate mechanism. The signaling is speculated to be transiently active and dialed down once adaptation is complete.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 represent recommendations for future work and mechanistic speculation. C85 appropriately identifies the need for developmental studies. C86 proposes a candidate mechanism with citation (van der Pijl et al., 2018), but the manuscript notes that expression analysis did not reveal consistent changes. C87 is speculation based on the age-independence of hypertrophy (C82-C83). These are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: Background on titin structure and function: Titin is the largest protein (~3800 kDa) spanning the half-sarcomere from Z-disk to M-band, with an I-band region functioning as a molecular spring consisting of tandem Ig and PEVK segments with different biophysical properties. Titin maintains sarcomere structural integrity and limits sarcomere length variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These are not novel findings of this study but provide necessary context. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to primary literature.

results.result: Background on controversy: While titin's contribution to single fiber passive stiffness is widely accepted, there are conflicting views on its relevance at the whole muscle level, with some proposing ECM dominance and others proposing titin dominance, with cardiac muscle showing titin dominance.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 accurately describe the controversy in the field that this study addresses. The claims are appropriately supported by citations representing different viewpoints. This establishes the rationale for the current study.

results.result: Background on disease relevance: Titin-based stiffness is altered in various muscle diseases, being increased in FSHD and cerebral palsy, and decreased in COPD diaphragm.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 provide clinical context with appropriate citations. These establish the translational relevance of understanding titin's role in passive stiffness.

results.result: The TtnΔ112-158 model provides a unique opportunity to test effects of altered titin-based tension on active muscle function.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is a valid statement about the utility of the model, supported by the subsequent experiments testing active function (C44-C46). The model does provide a unique tool for mechanistic studies.
